Two focus groups were conducted involving 17 participants, all hospitalized at the time of research for attempting suicide.

The aim of the present research was to gain insight, through the use of focus groups, into the individual experiences of patients who attempt suicide, in order to better understand, the causal reasons and emotions connected to a suicide attempt, and risk and protective factors with regard to possible repeat attempts and the attitude towards the assistance they receive.

Our study is, to our knowledge, the only one in the literature to involve suicidal patients in a research using focus group technique. The first aim of our study was to give voice to the real experience of suicidal patients so that what we recorded might aid us in better understanding the phenomenon.

The aim of this study is to gain insight into the individual experiences of patients who attempt suicide in order to better understand the reasons for and emotions behind a suicide attempt, thus also gaining insight, through the patients' own input, into the risk and protective factors which might influence possible repeat attempts and the attitude towards the assistance they receive. The main findings suggest that the relational factor represents a key point both as a trigger for the suicide attempt and for promoting the communication of the intent or for preventing a repeat suicide attempt, as interpersonal relationships and an empathic environment were, in essence, what was perceived as therapeutic and protective and enabled the expression of thoughts and self-understanding.

evidence.section_title: Risk and protective factors in repeat suicide attempts
evidence.quote: All patients indicated the period immediately after the attempt, including the realization of failure, as particularly high risk, as it is also characterized by rapidly changing emotions and feelings, which might easily trigger unpredictable and impulsive reactions. They identified as particularly risky, moments such as the beginning of hospitalization and the first few months after discharge: --- On the other hand, admission to hospital, an adequate pharmacological treatment, the feeling of empathy from caregivers and family members and regular and continuous monitoring from care givers immediately after discharge from hospital (this latter the most important and probably the only really protective and preventive factor) were believed to be among the protective factors:

Not only were patients pleased with being involved in the analysis of their own illness and care plan, but they turned out to be competent and expert in indicating, for example, risk factors (such as alcohol abuse, loneliness, depression, poor compliance to treatment, frequent interpersonal conflicts), the high-risk period with regard to preventive interventions, very similar to those proposed in the literature. The predominant trigger for a suicide attempt, even within the context of a psychiatric disorder, is in fact a difficulty or conflict within the family or a sentimental relationship. What seems to define the relational character of suicide is that any separation or loss is unbearable, and all patients are afraid of being left alone, of being gradually surrounded by and then submerged in a growing and inexorable feeling of loneliness and emptiness. It was noted that patients were perfectly capable of talking about themselves when they were encouraged to do so, within a supportive environment, and that their initial reticence was overcome, giving way to verbal expression of their suffering and satisfaction at having their words valued. For this reason, as suggested by patients, it is necessary to bear in mind the role of the relational factor throughout the therapeutic process, both at the moment of the admission, and in the outpatient treatment it seems appropriate to provide for those patients who have attempted suicide non-pharmacological treatment such as psychotherapy, non-specific relationship 'monitoring' or tutored self-help groups, as well as psychopharmacological treatment. Continuous monitoring after discharge from hospital, the need for constant 'emotional' assistance and the provision of an environment in which to be listened to are seen as priorities. Guided self-help interventions, through interaction may also assist in decreasing feelings of helplessness and the exclusiveness of one's suffering, which together constitute a common obstacle to communication.

The main findings of our study suggest that the relational factor represents a key point both as a trigger for the suicide attempt and for promoting the communication of the intent or for preventing a repeat suicide attempt, because interpersonal relationships and an empathic environment were, in essence, what was perceived as therapeutic and protective and enabled the expression of thoughts and self-understanding.
